title: Faith, pizza and the search for God

body.caption: Brother Nicholas Smith, from left, and Brother Benedict Dyar talk about monastic life in the monastery.

body.p: The life of a Benedictine monk might not be what most people imagine. There are no hooded figures lurking in dark corners — and certainly no shortage of personalities under the habit.

At St. Bernard Abbey in Cullman, Brother Benedict Dyar and Brother Nicholas Smith have discovered that monastic life brings its share of prayer, work, personal discipline and community — along with artistic pursuits, movie nights, occasional frustrations and an enduring appreciation for good pizza.

For the two monks, life together is more than sharing a home and a daily schedule. It is a way of seeking God, learning to live with others and finding support in a community whose members share a common purpose, even when they disagree or get on one another’s nerves.
Living in a community is “the hardest part,” Brother Nicholas said of monastic life. “It’s also the best.”

The same people who sometimes challenge a monk’s patience are the ones who pray alongside him, offer encouragement and help him through difficult moments. That tension between the challenges and blessings of living together lies at the heart of their Benedictine vocation.
Neither Brother Benedict nor Brother Nicholas followed a conventional path straight into religious life.

Before becoming a monk, Brother Benedict spent years as a musician. A drummer, he played in marching and jazz bands as well as several rock bands. He loved his drum kit and embraced the look that went with the music.
“I had the hair, I had everything, but the tattoos,” he said.
The thought of becoming a Benedictine monk first interested him when he was 19, but he did not seriously pursue it until he became Catholic in 2004, at age 24.

Brother Nicholas, meanwhile, pursued a career in education. He taught art in the Madison area at James Clemens and Bob Jones high schools before returning to his hometown, where he spent two years teaching painting and ceramics.
He still draws and paints in his spare time, finding room for creativity within a life structured around prayer and communal responsibilities.
And, as to what surprised him most about becoming a monk, Brother Nicholas pointed not to the schedule or the religious practices, but to the people.

He has come to appreciate the genuineness of the community, including the variety of personalities and interests represented among its members. Some are people he might never have encountered in ordinary life, he said, yet they come together around a common goal.
That shared purpose does not erase individual differences. Instead, it gives the monks a reason to work through them.
Community life can be both a source of frustration and a source of strength.
Brother Benedict said one of his frustrations is that even in an environment built on community, monks, like other people, can struggle to communicate directly.

Brother Nicholas has a more practical complaint. Someone who takes particular care with cleaning and organization, he finds it frustrating when a communal space is tidied up only to become messy again moments later.
His experience as an art teacher taught him that lesson, too. After students cleaned a room — or he cleaned it himself — the space would inevitably get dirty again.
“It’s the nature of anything,” he said.

But the nature of monastic life, living in such a structured environment, means that even free time can take some getting used to. Brother Benedict explained that monks become so accustomed to routine and schedules that an entirely open afternoon can feel less like a luxury than an unfamiliar void.
He often uses an unstructured afternoon to clean his room and listen to music.
Brother Nicholas turns to books, alternating between fiction and theology, or devotes weekend time to art.

His recent work includes a series of paintings depicting soldier saints. He has completed works featuring St. Joan of Arc and St. Maurice, a Roman soldier from the fourth century, and is working on St. George and his dragon. He hopes to complete two more pieces for the series.
The artwork does not always find an immediate home. Some pieces sit in his room for a while, though a portrait he made of Brother Joseph Zoettl has been placed at the Ave Maria Grotto.

Such pursuits offer glimpses of the individual interests that continue to flourish within a shared religious life. The monks have their assignments and obligations, but they also make room for creativity and recreation.

body.h: More than prayer in the choir

body.p: One misconception Brother Nicholas encounters is that monks spend virtually their entire day praying in church.
They do spend considerable time in prayer, but their lives encompass other aspects as well.
They have work assignments and chores, sometimes spend time together socially, go for walks and hold a movie night once a week — except during Lent.
Brother Benedict also challenged the familiar cinematic image of monks practicing severe penances, surviving on a crust of bread and a bottle of water, or inhabiting shadowy corners in hooded robes.
When his parents learned he was considering monastic life, they were worried. They imagined hooded figures holding candles and chanting Latin in dark corners.
That picture, Brother Benedict said, was an inaccurate depiction of the life he entered.
The reality includes ordinary human needs, personal interests and the daily work of living alongside other people. It also includes the discipline that makes the community possible.
“The good of all concerned, however, may prompt us to a little strictness in order to amend faults and to safeguard love,” as St. Benedict tells his monks in the Rule.
For Brother Nicholas, one tradition he hopes will never disappear is the chanting of the Divine Office.
“It’s beautiful, it’s peaceful,” he said. “It’s just amazing.”
The chanting, he said, is a source of continuity and beauty within the community’s rhythm of prayer.

But the hardest part of Benedictine life? Brother Nicholas returned to community. Differences must be navigated, conversations approached carefully and conflicts worked through. Yet those same relationships provide companionship and spiritual support.

The monks pray for one another and stand beside one another in times of struggle. Sometimes, Brother Nicholas observed, the person helping a monk through a struggle may also be the person with whom he is struggling.
Brother Benedict identified obedience as his greatest challenge. It requires a daily decision to surrender one’s own preferences and will to another person and to God.
Human beings naturally want to do things their own way, he said, and monks are no exception.
Brother Benedict also reflected on the vows associated with monastic life, including poverty and celibacy, while emphasizing the continuing demands of obedience.
For him, however, those demands do not diminish the privilege of his vocation.
“I cannot fathom any better life for myself than this one,” he said.
He recalled how unusual his path to the monastery seemed, and he believes God called him to it.
The most enjoyable part of his life, he said, is resting in the privilege of that calling and knowing that God loves him.
That sense of vocation also shapes how the monks understand people beyond the monastery.
Brother Benedict said he has learned that people often carry an emptiness they try to fill with things other than God. He has heard people tell him they want what he has.
His response is that they do not have to become monks to find it.
“You may not get the Office and the cloister and all that,” he tells them, “but you can have the Lord.”
For Brother Nicholas, the lesson for young people is to remain open to God’s direction rather than becoming too attached to a carefully mapped-out future.

He had planned from high school to become an art teacher, envisioned his ideal classroom and worked toward that goal. After achieving it, he realized he had not been listening closely enough to what God might be calling him to do.
“You can make all the plans you want,” he said, “but He has a plan that’s far better.”
The monks’ lives are not without humor.

Brother Nicholas has been asked whether he is a Sith Lord and has had people mistake his habit for a costume. Such encounters, particularly when he visits family or goes out with friends, can bring strange looks and unexpected questions. Brother Benedict has faced a similar pop-culture comparison.
But both monks say they welcome such opportunities to explain their vocation and talk about Christ. What begins as an awkward encounter can become a chance to evangelize.
And when the monks imagine an outing for the whole community, their minds turn not to an elaborate steakhouse dinner or a seafood restaurant, but to a pizzeria.

They may occasionally receive donated money for pizza, but Brother Benedict, if he had the opportunity, would take the community to visit a proper pizzeria. Brother Nicholas remembers gathering with friends back home around a 48-inch pizza from a hometown restaurant.

That conversation offers a lighthearted reminder that monks do not cease to be people when they enter the monastery. They retain their tastes, humor, frustrations and affection for the ordinary pleasures of life.

Brother Benedict hopes people will understand that monks are human beings, too. They have good days and bad days. They are not perfect, he said, but sinners striving to become holy through God’s grace.
That striving is the point.

Brother Nicholas admires Brother Benedict’s attentiveness to prayer and the way he expresses care through small gestures, such as checking in on a confrere or offering a word of appreciation. Brother Benedict, in turn, praises Brother Nicholas’ diligence in monastic observance and his creativity, particularly his willingness to find activities the community can enjoy together.

Their mutual respect reflects something deeper than compatibility. It is the work of a shared vocation, practiced through daily routines, prayer, personal sacrifice and the sometimes-difficult business of living with other people.

The monastery offers no escape from human imperfection. Instead, Brother Benedict and Brother Nicholas say it gives the monks a community in which to confront it, a tradition through which to pray and a common purpose that brings them back together.
And if that life occasionally leaves them wishing for a better pizza or a cleaner common room, those ordinary frustrations are part of the picture, too.

title: St. Bernard receives two international awards

body.p: Two international awards are coming home to St. Bernard Preparatory School after a strong performance at the global School Stories Awards.

Hosted by the London-based communications firm Interactive Schools, the competition recognizes excellence in creative filmmaking and digital storytelling on school websites. St. Bernard won first place for Best Alumni Story, a highly coveted award and a silver for Best Use of Video. The winning feature documents the lives of Dr. Andy Woods and Dr. Mackenzie Woods, following their journey from St. Bernard students to married doctors raising their son, Scotty, while highlighting how the school’s math and science faculty inspired their careers in chemistry.

body.caption: The Woods family, St. Bernard alumni, are featured in one of the school’s internationally recognized films.

body.p: “Their story demonstrates the lasting impact that our faculty and academic programs can have on students long after they graduate,” SBP Vice President Rachael Stover said.

St. Bernard earned the gold distinction in the category; McCallie School received silver and Beverly Hills High School earned bronze. The school also won a silver award in Best Use of Video for its “Created for Greater Things” video, highlighting its academic offerings, community and student experience.

The videos demonstrate St. Bernard Preparatory School’s distinctive mix of intellectual development, close community and familial environment. The selected alumni story perfectly reflects both the academic opportunities and lasting relationships students form on campus.

“We wanted viewers to see that St. Bernard is a place where students are encouraged to discover their passions, pursue their interests and build the academic foundation they need to succeed beyond high school,” Stover said.
The winners were announced during a live awards presentation that Stover attended remotely. She accepted both awards for St. Bernard Preparatory School.
“It was a pleasure to receive the awards on behalf of St. Bernard Prep,” Stover said. “You could feel the energy from the Interactive Schools presenters.”

St. Bernard alumni worked with outside partners to produce the videos. Alumnus and Emmy-nominated editor Glenn Gapultos led post-production, while alumna Lisa Proohet O’Brien directed the visual design and styling. Greg Jeffery, founder of the Catholic Development Group, supported the project throughout production.
The production took three full days of filming and involved current students, faculty, staff and alums.
“Seeing the St. Bernard community come together to tell these stories was meaningful. Having those stories recognized internationally makes the achievement even more special,” Stover said.
School leaders anticipate that international recognition will strengthen St. Bernard’s marketing and help prospective families better understand its mission and identity.

As a small boarding school, St. Bernard provides personal attention and the benefits of a close-knit campus community while maintaining a global perspective through a diverse student body from across the United States and abroad. “St. Bernard is more than a school,” Stover said. “It is a community and a family, one that challenges students intellectually, encourages them to pursue their passions and prepares them to make an impact in the world.”

title: Unsung Heroes: SBP’s bus drivers
byline: Grayson Stewart, staff writer for the Bernardian Herald

body.p: Editor’s note: The following story is an exclusive to St. Bernard Happenings from Dr. Craig Mann’s journalism class at St. Bernard Preparatory School. There are many unsung heroes around St. Bernard Prep who keep our school running every day. One special group of those individuals is the drivers who both connect SBP to families in the Decatur area each school day and transport our sports teams throughout the athletic seasons.

body.caption: Alan Kerber

body.p: Besides driving for SBP, Alan Kerber is the husband of Kimberly Kerber, whom he married in December 1978. He has four children who attended Sacred Heart and St. Bernard Preparatory School: Anne, Timothy, David, and Daniel. He also has eight grandchildren, including Madilyn, who graduated from SBP in 2024; Lily, an eighth grader at SBP; and Zoe, a fifth grader at Sacred Heart. In addition, Mr. Kerber has hosted three exchange students from Germany, all of whom attended St. Bernard.

Mr. Kerber was born and raised in Sidney, Ohio, where he was one of 12 children. He attended Catholic schools through his high school graduation. During high school, he worked 40 hours per week during his junior and senior years, and he also worked an eight-hour part-time job on Saturdays. After high school, Mr. Kerber became a cookie distributor for Archway, moving to Cullman with the company in 1987.

In 1995, he attended Wallace State Community College and later attended Athens State University, graduating with a bachelor’s degree in business. For the next 25 years after college, Mr. Kerber worked in sales and management. He then went to work at Cullman Caring for Kids, where he still works today as an inventory specialist and food bank manager.

In addition to working for Cullman Caring for Kids, Mr. Kerber is a regular bus driver for SBP and has driven for the Cullman County Board of Education since 2020. He was also the caretaker of the Catholic Cemetery from 2007 to 2025.
Mr. Kerber says that he likes to drive the bus because “I like the peace, quiet, and prayer time it gives me.”

He also offered some advice to the students at SBP: “Life will get hard, and when it does, put your head down, one foot in front of the other, and keep moving. Things either will get better or God will help you accept it; just keep moving forward.”

body.caption: Chief Kenny Culpepper

body.p: Chief Kenny Culpepper stays busy serving as both one of the school’s School Resource Officers and one of its bus drivers. The retired chief of the Cullman Police Department, Culpepper is married to Diane Culpepper, a retired schoolteacher. He is the father of three children — Cody, Clint and Kelsey — and a grandfather to two granddaughters, Olivia and Ophelia.

Chief Culpepper graduated from Cullman High School, where he was a star on the football team. From there, he attended Auburn University, where he majored in criminal justice and played on the rugby team. He later graduated from Athens State with degrees in history and political science.

He spent 21 years in the Alabama National Guard, serving in the 20th Special Forces. Shortly after this service, he also joined the Cullman Police Department, where he worked as an officer for 48 years and served as chief for 34. When he retired in 2022, Chief Culpepper was hired at SBP as an SRO, a role he has held for four years. Besides driving St. Bernard Prep’s school buses, he also drives for Cullman City Schools and St. John’s Church.
In his rare free time, Chief Culpepper likes to work on his farm and attend Auburn football games.
“My favorite thing is spending time with my family,” he said. “On Wednesday nights, we have family night. Our kids and grandkids come over and we eat and play games.”

“I really enjoy working at St. Bernard,” Chief Culpepper added. “The students are great. I taught D.A.R.E. (Drug Abuse Resistance Education) here for 20-plus years with (longtime educator) Ruth Ann Knight, and it has always been a special place to me.”

body.caption: Shaun Stewart

body.p: Shaun Stewart, a familiar face around Saint Bernard, has been driving the Decatur bus route Tuesday through Friday afternoons for a year.

Aside from driving the bus, Mr. Stewart is married to Kim Stewart and has two children, Griffin and Grayson. In 1997, he graduated from Vinemont High School after playing football for six years. He then attended Wallace State Community College, where he was active in the machine shop program. He has worked as a conductor for CSX Railroad in Decatur and Birmingham for 26 years.
In his free time, Mr. Stewart enjoys watching Alabama football, helping his wife in the classroom and spending time with his family.

“St. Bernard has become a big part of our family and lives,” Mr. Stewart said. “I’ve enjoyed helping with the festivals and getting to know most of the staff, and I’ve also enjoyed interacting with the students who ride the bus.”

title: Anabelle Howze brings storytelling experience to St. Bernard

body.caption: Anabelle Howze

body.p: For Anabelle Howze, joining St. Bernard Preparatory School has been an opportunity to put her communications experience to work in a community whose mission reflects her faith.

A Cullman native, Howze earned a bachelor’s degree in mass communications from the University of North Alabama, graduating a year and a half early. She focused on broadcasting and journalism. An internship in strategic marketing and communications at the UAB School of Nursing gave her experience sharing the work of a higher education institution.

Howze later worked as a multimedia journalist at The Cullman Tribune, covering local news and community events. In July, she joined St. Bernard as its Marketing and Events Coordinator. Howze now oversees festival planning and helps tell St. Bernard’s story through school publications, social media and more. Her work also supports admissions and connects the school with the wider community.

One of her first major responsibilities was helping organize the 10th annual Bernard Blues & BBQ Festival. Without a formal background in event planning, taking on a festival that size was daunting at first. Working alongside experienced colleagues gave her a chance to learn as preparations came together.

What resonated most with Howze was the team’s devotion to St. Bernard and its festivals. Teamwork with people so focused on keeping those traditions alive and growing ended up being the highlight of her first festival.

Howze considers it a privilege to work at a school where faith guides daily life and service to others reflects a commitment to honoring God. The welcome she has received from those who carry out that mission has deepened her appreciation for St. Bernard.
She looks forward to sharing the community’s stories and helping its traditions grow, while continuing to learn from the people who have made her feel at home.
